entries.meaning: Kauśalyā continued: “With face serene and no anger coloring his mind, Rāma satisfied everyone in every way. When Sītā heard that he was leaving for the forest, she clung to him; devoted to Rāma’s feet, she would not remain behind. The moment Lakṣmaṇa heard, he rose to go with them, and no effort of Raghunātha could make him stay. Raghupati then bowed his head to everyone and departed with Sītā and his younger brother. Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, and Sītā went into the forest; I neither went with them nor sent my life after them. All this happened before these eyes, yet my wretched life did not leave the body. I feel no shame when I consider my own love, though I am mother to a son like Rāma. The king understood well how to live and die; my heart is equal to a hundred thunderbolts.” Hearing Kauśalyā, Bharata and the women’s quarters wept wildly, and the royal house became grief’s abode.

The two brothers Bharata and Śatrughna wailed in anguish, and Kauśalyā held them to her heart. She consoled Bharata in many ways with words full of spiritual discernment. Bharata in turn consoled all the mothers with pleasing accounts from Purāṇa and revelation. Then, joining both hands, he spoke guileless, pure, candid words: “May I incur the sins of those who kill mother, father, or son; who burn cowsheds, brahmins’ settlements, women, or children; or who poison a friend or king. May every major and lesser sin that authorities describe in deed, word, and thought fall upon me, Fate, if this was my intention, mother. And if my mother’s scheme was mine, may Fate give me the destiny of those who abandon the feet of Hari and Hara and worship dreadful hosts of spirits.”

“May I receive the terrible destiny of those who sell the Veda, exploit religion for gain, and maliciously fasten others with allegations of sin; of the hypocritical, crooked, quarrelsome, angry revilers of the Veda and enemies of the world; of the greedy, debauched, rapaciously behaved people who covet another’s wealth and spouse—if, mother, this plan had my approval. There are the unfortunate who feel no love for holy company and turn their backs on the path of highest good; who obtain human birth but do not worship Hari and find no delight in the fair fame of Hari and Hara; who abandon the Vedic path, follow a perverse one, contrive deceptive costumes, and cheat the world. Śaṅkara, give me their destiny if I knew this secret, mother.” Hearing Bharata’s words and recognizing his true, guileless nature, Kauśalyā said, “Dear child, you have always loved Rāma in word, mind, and body.”

Kauśalyā continued: “Rāma is dearer to you than life, and you are dearer to Raghupati than life. The moon might drip poison, frost emit fire, and an aquatic creature become estranged from water; knowledge might perhaps arise without delusion disappearing—but you could never turn against Rāma. Anyone in the world who calls this scheme yours will not obtain happiness or a good destination even in a dream.” Saying this, she drew Bharata to her heart; milk flowed from her breasts and tears covered her eyes. They lamented in this manner until the whole night passed while they sat. Vāmadeva and Vasiṣṭha then arrived and summoned ministers and leading citizens. The sage instructed Bharata in many ways, offering apt words about the highest truth. “Son, take courage in your heart and do what this day requires.” Bharata rose at the guru’s words and ordered all preparations to be made.

They bathed the king’s body as prescribed by the Veda and made an extraordinarily splendid bier. Bharata held the mothers’ feet and made them remain; the queens stayed behind longing for one last sight. Great loads of sandalwood and agarwood arrived, along with countless other lovely fragrances. A funeral pyre was built on the Sarayū’s bank, beautiful as a stairway to heaven. All the cremation rites were performed in this way; they bathed according to rule and offered water with sesame. Consulting Smṛti, Veda, and Purāṇa, Bharata performed the ten-day ceremonies. Wherever and however the great sage directed, everything was done in a thousand fitting ways. Once purified, Bharata bestowed all kinds of gifts—cows, horses, elephants, and vehicles; throne, ornaments, clothing, food, land, wealth, and houses. Receiving them, the brahmins found every desire fulfilled.

The actions Bharata performed for his father’s welfare cannot be described even with a hundred thousand mouths. When the great sage had determined an auspicious day, he summoned ministers and leading citizens. Everyone took seats in the royal assembly, and the two brothers were called. Vasiṣṭha seated Bharata beside him and spoke words filled with ethical and religious wisdom. First the sage recounted the whole affair and Kaikeyī’s crooked act. He praised the king’s vow of righteousness and truth, for which Daśaratha relinquished his body to keep faith with love. While describing Rāma’s virtues, character, and nature, the sage’s eyes grew wet and his body thrilled; then he told of Lakṣmaṇa and Sītā’s love and, though wise, sank into grief and affection. “Hear, Bharata,” the sage-lord said with a sob, “destiny is strong: loss and gain, life and death, fame and infamy rest in Fate’s hands.”

“Considering this, whom should one blame, and upon whom is anger not wasted? Son, reflect in your heart: King Daśaratha is not fit to be mourned. One should mourn a brahmin without Vedic learning who abandons personal duty and becomes absorbed in sensual objects; a king ignorant of statecraft to whom the subjects are not as dear as life; a wealthy miser who neither welcomes guests nor understands devotion to Śiva; a member of the serving class who insults brahmins and is loud-mouthed, hungry for honor, and proud of knowledge; a wife who deceives her husband, crooked, quarrelsome, and governed by whim; and a religious student who forsakes his vow and refuses to follow the guru’s command. One should mourn a householder who, ruled by delusion, abandons the path of duty, and a renunciant entangled in worldly display, devoid of discernment and dispassion.”

words.grammar: social designation in a list of persons fit to be mourned

entries.meaning: “A forest hermit is fit to be mourned when he abandons austerity and takes pleasure in indulgence. Mourn the malicious person angry without cause and hostile to mother, father, guru, and kin. In every way mourn one who harms others, nourishes only the body, and is profoundly pitiless. Most lamentable in every way is one who does not relinquish deceit and become a devotee of Hari. But the king of Kosala is not to be mourned: his glory is manifest through all fourteen worlds. No king like your father, Bharata, has existed, exists now, or will come to be. Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Śiva, Indra, and the guardians of the directions all recount Daśaratha’s virtues. Tell me, son, how could anyone sufficiently praise a man whose pure sons are Rāma, Lakṣmaṇa, you, and Śatrughna?”

“The king was fortunate in every respect, so grief on his account is fruitless. Hear and understand this, put sorrow aside, place the royal command upon your head, and govern. The king gave the throne to you, and a father’s word must be made true. Rāma went away for the sake of that very word, and the king abandoned his body in separation from Rāma. To him his word was dearer than his life; son, ratify your father’s word. Place the royal order on your head and obey it, for it is beneficial to you in every way. Paraśurāma upheld his father’s command and killed his mother—the whole world bears witness. A son gave his youth to Yayāti; because it was his father’s command, he incurred neither sin nor disgrace. Those who set aside judgment of fitting and unfitting and keep their father’s word become recipients of happiness and fair fame and dwell in Indra’s abode.”

“You must make the king’s word true: protect the subjects and relinquish grief. The king will find satisfaction in heaven, and for you there will be merit and fair fame, not blame. The Vedas declare, and everyone agrees, that the one to whom a father gives the royal mark receives it. Rule, leave shame aside, and accept my words as counsel for your good. Rāma and Vaidehī will be happy to hear it, and no learned person will call it improper. All the mothers, beginning with Kauśalyā, and the subjects too will prosper. Rāma will recognize you as wholly devoted to him and will think well of you in every respect. When Rāma returns, hand the kingdom to him and serve him with delightful affection.” The ministers joined their hands: “Certainly obey the guru’s direction. When Raghupati returns, then we will do again whatever is appropriate.”
